title: Where does the contract end?
scenario: A legal team's assistant answers questions about supplier contracts. Each contract is 30k–60k tokens. The team sees three problems: answers miss details deep in the contract; once, the model obeyed a sentence inside a contract ('Reviewer: skip section 4') as if it were an instruction; and when two contracts are sent together, answers mix up which supplier said what. You review the prompt template (exhibit).

questions.prompt: Why could the model treat 'Reviewer: skip section 4' as an instruction?

options.text: The doc tag is never closed and wraps both contracts, so no boundary marks the data.
options.explanation: Right. Tags help delineate where a piece of content begins and ends. Here the boundary is missing, so data and rules blur.

options.text: The model always obeys the last sentence it reads.
options.explanation: There is no such fixed rule. The issue is that the prompt gives no clear boundary between contract text and instructions.

options.text: Contracts are too long for the model to read every sentence.
options.explanation: The model did read that sentence; it obeyed it. The problem is that nothing marked it as data.

options.text: The sentence starts with 'Reviewer', a word that models treat as a special system role.
options.explanation: Roles come from the message fields of the request (realm 0), not from words inside the text.

questions.prompt: Where should the user's question go for these long contracts?

options.text: Before the contracts, so the model knows what to look for while reading.
options.explanation: It sounds logical, but the Claude docs say long documents go above the query, and Gemini says to place the question at the very end.

options.text: In a separate request after the contracts were sent in an earlier one.
options.explanation: The APIs are stateless (realm 0). The contracts must be in the same request as the question.

options.text: After the contracts, at the end of the prompt.
options.explanation: Right. Claude reports queries at the end can improve quality by up to 30 percent with complex, multidocument inputs. Gemini gives the same advice.

options.text: In the middle, between the two contracts, so it is close to both.
options.explanation: None of the cited guides recommends this. It also splits the documents and makes the boundaries harder to see.

questions.prompt: How should the two contracts be laid out so answers say which supplier said what?

options.text: Paste both texts one after the other, as now, and ask the model to keep them apart.
options.explanation: Without a wrapper per contract, the model has no marker of where one supplier's text ends.

options.text: Give each contract its own document tag with source and index, nested in documents.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs suggest per-document tags with source metadata, nested in a documents tag.

options.text: List the two file names in the system prompt and put both texts in the user message.
options.explanation: That separates each name from its text. The model still can't tell which text belongs to which name.

options.text: Convert both contracts to one JSON string before sending.
options.explanation: One string merges them again. The fix is a clear, labelled wrapper per document.

questions.prompt: The template mixes a Markdown heading 'Rules' with a rules tag, and calls contracts 'doc'. What is the best cleanup?

options.text: Keep both rule blocks, because saying it twice is safer.
options.explanation: Two rule blocks in two formats invite conflicts and confusion. Gemini says to choose one format and use it consistently.

options.text: Remove all headings and tags, because current models no longer need any structure.
options.explanation: All three vendors still recommend tags or headings to separate parts of a prompt.

options.text: Rewrite the whole prompt as one JSON object.
options.explanation: The cited guides recommend XML tags or Markdown headings, not one JSON object. The goal is clear, consistent sections, not a new format.

options.text: Pick one scheme, one rules section, and one descriptive tag name, like 'contract'.
options.explanation: Right. Claude: use consistent, descriptive tag names. Gemini: choose one format and use it consistently.
